title: Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR
summary: How does the compiler decide what a name refers to? **Unqualified lookup** searches outwards through scopes. **ADL** also searches the namespaces of the arguments' types, which is why `std::cout << x` finds `std::operator<<`. **Inline namespaces** version an interface. The **One Definition Rule** keeps definitions consistent across the program.
markdown:
## Lookup comes first Before a call is resolved, three things happen in a fixed order. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["1. Name lookup
find candidate declarations"] --> B["2. Overload resolution
choose the best match"] --> C["3. Access check
is it public here?"] ``` A surprising amount of C++ behaviour follows from that order. A function that would be a perfect match is never considered if lookup does not find it, and a private function can win overload resolution and then be rejected. ## Unqualified lookup A name written without `::` is searched for from the innermost scope outwards. ``` namespace app { int x; searched third namespace ui { int x; searched second void f() { int x; searched first: found, so the search stops use(x); } } } ``` The search **stops at the first scope that contains the name**. It does not go on to see whether an outer scope has a better candidate. That is the mechanism behind name hiding in derived classes ([[8.02 Inheritance and Access]]), where one function in the derived class hides every base overload of the same name. A **qualified** name, such as `app::x` or `::x`, is looked up only in the scope named. ## Argument-dependent lookup For an unqualified **function call**, there is a second search. ```cpp #include namespace geo { struct Point { int x{}; int y{}; }; void print(const Point& p) { std::cout << p.x << ',' << p.y << '\n'; } } int main() { const geo::Point p{ 1, 2 }; print(p); // found without writing geo:: return 0; } ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR C["print(p)"] --> U["ordinary lookup:
the enclosing scopes"] C --> A["ADL: the namespaces of
the argument types.
p is a geo::Point, so search geo"] U & A --> O["overload resolution over
everything found"] ``` **Argument-dependent lookup** (ADL) adds, for each argument, the namespace in which its type is defined. The functions found both ways are combined into one set of candidates. The motivation is operators. `std::cout << text` must find `std::operator<<(std::ostream&, const std::string&)`. Nobody wants to write `std::operator<<(std::cout, text)`. ADL makes a type's interface include the free functions in its namespace. ### The two-step swap Generic code that swaps should use a type's own `swap` if it provides one, and `std::swap` otherwise. ```cpp template void exchange(T& a, T& b) { using std::swap; // makes std::swap a candidate swap(a, b); // unqualified: ADL adds any swap in T's namespace } ``` | Written as | Finds | |---|---| | `std::swap(a, b)` | Only `std::swap`. A type's optimized `swap` is ignored. | | `swap(a, b)` alone | Only what ADL finds. Fails for `int`, which has no namespace. | | `using std::swap; swap(a, b);` | Both, and overload resolution prefers the more specific | `std::ranges::swap` performs this dance for you. > [!warning] ADL works when you did not ask for it > An unqualified call can select a function from an argument's namespace that you have never heard of. In generic code, qualify calls that you do **not** intend to be customisable: write `std::move`, `std::forward` and `std::addressof` in full. ### Hidden friends A friend function **defined inside** a class is not visible to ordinary lookup at all. It can be found **only** by ADL, when one of the arguments has that class type. ```cpp struct Vec2 { double x{}; double y{}; friend Vec2 operator+(Vec2 a, Vec2 b) { return { a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y }; } }; ``` | Benefit | Why | |---|---| | Smaller overload sets | The operator is a candidate only when a `Vec2` is involved | | Fewer accidental conversions | It cannot be selected through an implicit conversion of some unrelated type | | Faster compilation, clearer errors | The compiler has fewer candidates to consider and report | This is the recommended way to write operators, and what the examples in [[6.07 Operator Overloading Basics]] were quietly doing. ## Inline namespaces The members of an **inline namespace** are treated as members of the enclosing namespace too. ```cpp namespace lib { namespace v1 { void parse(); } inline namespace v2 { void parse(); } } lib::parse(); // v2, the current version lib::v1::parse(); // the old version, still reachable ``` Libraries use this for **versioning**. Callers write `lib::parse` and get whichever version is marked `inline`; the version name is still part of each symbol, so code built against different versions cannot be linked together by mistake. The standard library's literal suffixes live in inline namespaces, which is why `using namespace std::chrono_literals;` and `using namespace std::literals;` both work. ## Unnamed namespaces ```cpp namespace { int helper() { return 1; } } ``` Everything in an unnamed namespace has **internal linkage**: it is private to its source file ([[3.06 Global Variables, static and Linkage]]). Unlike `static`, it applies to types as well as to functions and variables, which matters for the next section. ## The One Definition Rule The **One Definition Rule** (ODR) has three parts. | Scope | Rule | |---|---| | Within one translation unit | An entity is defined at most once | | Across the whole program | A non-inline function or variable that is used is defined **exactly once** | | Classes, templates, inline functions and inline variables | May be defined in several translation units, but every definition must be **identical**, token for token and in meaning | A **translation unit** is one source file after all its `#include`s have been pasted in. The third rule is the dangerous one. ``` a.cpp: struct Config { int width; int height; }; b.cpp: struct Config { int width; int height; int depth; }; Each file compiles. The program links. No error, no warning. Code in a.cpp and b.cpp now disagree about the size and layout of a Config. ``` A violation of this kind is "ill-formed, no diagnostic required". The linker sees two things called `Config` and assumes they are the same. The result is memory corruption that appears far from its cause. | How it happens | Defence | |---|---| | Two source files each define a helper class with the same name | Put file-local types in an unnamed namespace | | Two libraries define the same name in the global namespace | Give every library its own namespace | | A header is included with different macros defined beforehand | Avoid macros that alter definitions | | Object files built with different settings that change layouts | Build everything with the same options | | An inline function in a header that behaves differently per file | Keep headers free of dependence on file-local context | Modules ([[13.05 Modules (C++20) and import std (C++23)]]) remove much of this class of problem: a module's entities are attached to that module, so same-named entities in different modules do not collide. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Why does `std::cout << "hi"` work without writing `std::operator<<`? + Argument-dependent lookup searches `std`, home of `cout`'s type - Because `operator<<` is a keyword - Because `` adds `using namespace std;` - Because operators are always global > ADL looks in the namespaces of the arguments' types, so it finds the `operator<<` declared in `std`. ? What makes violations of the One Definition Rule so dangerous? - The compiler rejects them with confusing messages - They make the program slower + They are usually not diagnosed at all - They only happen in Release builds > Two different definitions with the same name in different files can silently pick either one, with no error. ? Why write `using std::swap;` before an unqualified `swap(a, b)`? - Because `swap` is not in `std` otherwise - To force `std::swap` to be called + `std::swap` becomes a fallback while ADL can find a better one - To stop ADL from looking anywhere > This "two-step" lets a type's own efficient `swap` win when it exists, and uses `std::swap` when it does not. ? How can a hidden friend be found? - By ordinary unqualified lookup from anywhere - By qualifying it with the class name - By including the header twice + Only through argument-dependent lookup > A friend defined inside the class is not visible to normal lookup. That keeps overload sets small and avoids surprises. ```
ideas:
1. Put a `print(const T&)` in a namespace of your own and call it unqualified. Then break it by declaring a nearer `print(int)` in the calling scope.
2. Give a class a custom `swap` in its namespace and verify that the two-step idiom calls it.
3. Turn an operator defined outside a class into a hidden friend and check which calls still compile.

cards.a:
Argument-dependent lookup searches `std`, home of `cout`'s type

ADL looks in the namespaces of the arguments' types, so it finds the `operator<<` declared in `std`.

cards.q: What makes violations of the One Definition Rule so dangerous?
cards.a:
They are usually not diagnosed at all

Two different definitions with the same name in different files can silently pick either one, with no error.

cards.q: Why write `using std::swap;` before an unqualified `swap(a, b)`?
cards.a:
`std::swap` becomes a fallback while ADL can find a better one

This "two-step" lets a type's own efficient `swap` win when it exists, and uses `std::swap` when it does not.

cards.q: How can a hidden friend be found?
cards.a:
Only through argument-dependent lookup

A friend defined inside the class is not visible to normal lookup. That keeps overload sets small and avoids surprises.
